conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening we use with every new mom called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, designed to catch any signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after baby arrives.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the medical team directly involved in your care, so please feel comfortable answering as honestly as you can. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. We’ll go question by question, and I’ll re-phrase things in everyday language so it’s quick and easy.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

(sighs softly, eyes downcast)

Honestly... it’s been really hard. I used to laugh at little things all the time—my husband’s dumb jokes, cute videos—but now it feels like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. Even when I *want* to laugh, it just... doesn’t come. It’s like the joy got muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… not really. Most of the week I couldn’t.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I can’t really remember the last time I actually looked forward to anything. Even simple stuff—like my favorite show coming on or a walk with the baby—just feels like another chore I have to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a terrible mom.” I’ll replay every little thing—did I eat the wrong foods while nursing, did I pick her up too fast, too slow—and convince myself it’s my fault. Even when my husband says she’s just being a normal baby, I still feel like I should somehow be fixing it better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Almost every day. My mind keeps spinning “what-ifs” about her breathing, her color, whether she’s too hot or too cold. I’ll lie in bed checking the monitor every few minutes even though nothing’s wrong. I know it’s probably irrational, but I can’t turn the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes... like late at night when everything's quiet, this wave of fear just hits me out of nowhere. My chest gets tight, heart races, and suddenly I'm convinced something awful is about to happen to the baby. I know there's no real reason for it, but in those moments I feel completely terrified.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… quite a lot. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep when she finally sleeps, the never-ending laundry—it all piles up until I feel like I’m drowning. Some mornings I wake up already exhausted and think, “How am I going to get through today?” I manage, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… most nights. I’ll finally get her down, but then my mind just races—replaying everything I think I messed up, worrying about the next day, picturing worst-case scenarios. Even when I’m exhausted, I can’t shut it off, so I lie there staring at the ceiling or checking the monitor every ten minutes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy sadness that just sits with me, even when nothing specific is wrong. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be happier, but instead I feel empty and weepy. Some afternoons I end up crying while I’m folding her onesies, and I can’t always explain why—it’s just this constant gloom I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… most days this week. Sometimes it’s when she won’t settle and I feel useless, sometimes it’s just looking at her and feeling like I’m failing her somehow. The tears come out of nowhere—I'll be rocking her and suddenly I’m sobbing quietly so I don’t wake her. It’s like the sadness just overflows.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. I could never leave her like that.

You've shared how the joy you used to feel has been replaced by a heavy, daily sadness that makes even small pleasures feel impossible. You described constant worry about your baby, frequent tearfulness, overwhelming guilt when she fusses, and nights spent wide-awake with racing thoughts. Despite working hard to care for her, you feel you're barely keeping your head above water and worry you're failing as a mom.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient states she has not been able to laugh or see the funny side at all during the week, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses minimal to no anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "a lot of the time," ruminating over minor issues and feeling personally responsible for normal infant behavior, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries despite no objective threat, aligning with "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes experiencing sudden, unexplained fear/panic "sometimes" with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent struggle and feeling overwhelmed, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty on "most nights" with racing thoughts and constant worry, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, pervasive sadness with tearfulness and emptiness, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying "most days this week" and describes frequent, unprompted tearfulness that "overflows," matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the EPDS threshold of ≥14 that signals probable major depression. You endorse <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym> and <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, nearly every day, plus <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and <sym>diminished ability to concentrate</sym>, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The prominent anxiety symptoms suggest a mixed depression-anxiety presentation common after childbirth. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact your OB or primary care doctor today to discuss these results and arrange same-week evaluation
2. Ask about referral to a perinatal mental-health specialist and therapy options such as CBT or interpersonal therapy
3. Inquire about evidence-based medication compatible with breastfeeding if recommended
4. Arrange practical support-ask a trusted adult to help with night feeds or household tasks so you can rest
5. Practice brief self-care: five-minute outdoor walks, balanced snacks, and accepting help without guilt
6. Keep the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 in your phone for 24/7 emotional support
7. Return for re-screening in two weeks or sooner if thoughts worsen or self-harm ideas develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [licensed mental health professional]

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased):
- Marked anhedonia & inability to laugh (Q1, Q2)
- Daily pervasive sadness, frequent crying spells (Q8, Q9)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Clinically significant anxiety: near-constant worry, nocturnal panic attacks, somatic arousal (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm and functional impairment (Q6)
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe depressive symptoms accompanied by prominent anxiety; no current self-harm ideation (Q10 denied).

Screening significance:
- High depressive symptom count → elevated probability of major postpartum depression
- Co-occurring anxiety/panic symptoms suggest mixed depression-anxiety presentation
- Sleep disruption and guilt cognitions are additional risk factors for clinical worsening

Risk factors noted:
- Persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, daily tearfulness
- Sleep difficulties directly linked to ruminative mood
- Self-criticism and maternal guilt
- Anxiety symptoms causing distress and functional interference
- No expressed suicidal or infanticidal ideation at present

Summary: Screening indicates clinically significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms requiring prompt follow-up evaluation for diagnosis and possible intervention. Safety plan reviewed; patient denies current self-harm thoughts. Recommend expedited referral to OB mental-health team or outpatient psychiatric services.
